utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Good afternoon. Just before we start with the next witness, let me just mention that the Trial Chamber is seized of a motion for certification. It is pretty urgent. I don't know whether the Prosecution would be in a position to give an expedited response today sometime.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Your Honour, if -- it depends. Are we going to continue with the witness?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Yes, we are going to continue with the witness.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: In that case, we could provide -- because I can't do two things at once, we could provide a response certainly first thing tomorrow morning, if that's okay. I'm seeing shaking of the head.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HOEPFEL
utterances.text: That's too late.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Well, I -- I can't write a response while I'm in here doing a cross-examination.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: I appreciate that.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: So I can do it after court. And it won't take very long and I'm happy to file it after I finish it. I'll stay here and do it and file it when -- or provide it when it's done.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: You can't rely on any of your colleagues to help in the team?

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Well, I guess I could -- I could do that, if that's what the -- if the Trial Chamber wants a response today, then that's what we'll do. That's fine. I'll ask Mr. Black to step out and take charge of -- by the way, if I may, just as a matter of politeness, I'm sorry I didn't do this sooner. I'd like to just introduce Ms. Hanne Walker. She is an intern with the Office of the Prosecution who has been helping us on these matters in particular, so we have asked that she sit in the courtroom today. So that's why she's here.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Welcome to the courtroom. Maybe you could postpone your coming into the courtroom and draft the response and then come in after finishing that.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: I think what I'll' do, having read the body language from the Trial Chamber, if not the explicit statements from the Trial Chamber, I think I'll ask Mr. Black to excuse himself from the courtroom and to draft a response. And it's now 2.30, and I hope we can get it in buy 4 o'clock, but if not, we'll ask for the ability for a late filing and -- but we'll certainly get it in today.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you very much. The Chamber is indebted to you and appreciates the effort. We are trying to give this decision on certification today.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: I understand.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you very much. Mr. Milovancevic?

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honour. The Defence would like to inform the Trial Chamber that we are going to suspend our presentation of evidence until the question of the status of the expert findings. In result, we have two expert findings. One is an international law expert, this is Professor Avramov who is now in the Tribunal's office in Belgrade. We have her on the link now. We believe this is an exceptionally dramatic situation, as far as the Defence is concerned. Simply the way in which the introduction of the expert findings of Dr. Avramov has been permitted denies the Defence to deal with the series of questions that have been mentioned in the indictment. To be specific, these are paragraphs 18 and 20 of the indictment, in which --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Mr. Milovancevic, that argument, as we said to you, you'll put it on paper and put it before the Court. You don't need to go into that argument at all now verbally, because you want us now to look at the reasons why the report is redacted in the manner in which it's redacted and you want us to reconsider that. We cannot do that unless you submit a proper submission on that point. Let me say this: On the first two sentences or two of your introductory remarks, that I'm not quite sure what you mean by you're going to suspend, because you're asking for an appeal. Obviously, if your appeal succeeds, you will call this witness in full to the extent that the appeal court has granted you. For now, I would like us to proceed with the proceedings as this Trial Chamber has determined. Obviously, if you disagree with the finding of this Trial Chamber, as you have rightly done, your recourse is in the appeal court and to the extent that the appeal court comes to your rescue, you will repair what this court has done. Now I want to suggest that you consider seriously calling this witness so that we proceed now.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, thank you. I understand what you have said, and I am completely aware of the logic of that, especially when one has in mind the principle of the efficiency of the Court proceedings. What I'm saying now is not an attempt to provide arguments for our beginning sentence, but just to indicate to you the reasons why Defence has the position that it has. Your Honour, the expert findings of Professor Avramov do not contain her conclusion or the essence of her findings, in fact.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Mr. Milovancevic, I'm sorry. As I said to you, to the extent that the appeal court will come to your rescue, and allow those conclusions, to the extent we will repair that evidence at that time. At this point in time, this Trial Chamber has ruled in a particular way and we -- let us carry on the way this Trial Chamber has ruled. You cannot -- you cannot have your cake and eat it. You cannot ask for an appeal and then on the other hand say, I'm sorry, I'm not participating, unless you're closing your case. If you're closing your case, fine, close your case and go on appeal, but you can't hold the Trial Chamber to ransom, because this is what you're now doing.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, I would like the Trial Chamber to give us a 15-minute break so that the Defence team can consult Mr. Martic. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Court adjourned. We'll reconvene at quarter to 3.00. --- Break taken at 2.30 p.m.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Milovancevic?

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, after our consultation, I would like to inform the Trial Chamber that the Defence, in accordance with the suggestion of the Trial Chamber, will continue with its work today. Based on the decision on this matter by the Trial Chamber, regarding the testimony of Professor Smilja Avramov, I would like to add the following thing in order to have the Defence's position understood correctly. It was not our intention, Your Honours, to blackmail either the Trial Chamber or the Appeals Chamber. We simply believe that we are in the position, as a result of such editing of our expert reports, are in a position that is not to our full advantage and then we will have to see how to proceed on the basis of that. We are going to act on your instructions, since the Prosecution is in the process of drafting its response. So we will continue today with our work, with the remark that parts of the expert report by Professor Avramov relating to the mediation by the European Commission relating to recognition were direct response to the count 68 or paragraph 68 of the indictment. And in the indictment, the Prosecution states that as the basis for making an assessment of the situation, thus, we are not now in a position to be able to deal with that point, at the moment, at least. These are some of the reasons why we wanted to make our position clear. The examination-in-chief of the expert, Professor Avramov, will be conducted by my learned friend, Mr. Nikola Perovic.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you very much, Mr. Milovancevic. We have lost a lot of time. I hope we are going to finish with this witness in the time allocated. Mr. Perovic.

utterances.speaker: MR. PEROVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, I would like to summon as a Defence witness an expert witness of the Defence, Professor Smilja Avramov.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you very much, Mr. Perovic.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: May the witness please make the declaration. Is somebody helping the witness where she is? Because I see her lips moving, we don't hear sound and I don't see a face of a person from -- oh, thank you very much. There is somebody.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HOEPFEL
utterances.text: Sorry, we don't have sound.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I solemnly declare that I will speak the truth, the whole truth and nothing but the truth.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Witness answered through interpreter].

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you very much, ma'am. You may be seated. Yes, Mr. Perovic.

utterances.speaker: MR. PEROVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. PEROVIC
utterances.text: Good day, Madam Avramov.

utterances.speaker: SMILJA AVRAMOV
utterances.text: Good day.

utterances.speaker: MR. PEROVIC
utterances.text: Do you hear me well?

utterances.speaker: SMILJA AVRAMOV
utterances.text: Yes, very well.

utterances.speaker: MR. PEROVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Before I put some questions to you regarding your expert report, I would like to ask you to tell us briefly something about your career. I'm going to help you in that. You were born in 1918; is this correct?

utterances.speaker: SMILJA AVRAMOV
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. PEROVIC
utterances.text: You were born in?

utterances.speaker: SMILJA AVRAMOV
utterances.text: Pakrac, now in Croatia.

utterances.speaker: MR. PEROVIC
utterances.text: You completed the -- your secondary school, gymnasium?

utterances.speaker: SMILJA AVRAMOV
utterances.text: Yes, I graduated at the classical gymnasium and then later I studied law in Zagreb and in Vienna. And I defended my master's thesis, the standard of international economic law in Yugoslav practice. I obtained my Ph.D. in law in Belgrade, after defending my doctor's thesis. I published about ten books and about 200 research papers and scientific works.

utterances.speaker: MR. PEROVIC
utterances.text: You're a retired Professor of the law faculty of the university in Belgrade; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: SMILJA AVRAMOV
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. PEROVIC
utterances.text: How many years did you spend teaching as a Professor at the Belgrade university?

utterances.speaker: SMILJA AVRAMOV
utterances.text: For a full 39 years. And in the meantime, I taught at numerous universities in the country and abroad, from Japan to the United States, Germany, London and so on and so forth.

utterances.speaker: MR. PEROVIC
utterances.text: Were you a member of any international associations that dealt with international law?

utterances.speaker: SMILJA AVRAMOV
utterances.text: Yes. That is correct. I was the president of the Yugoslav Association for International Law, and then in 1980, I was elected as the president of the International Law Association. Other than that, I was the president of the International Confederation for Peace and Disarmament from 1968 until 1978. I was a member of other professional associations.

utterances.speaker: MR. PEROVIC
utterances.text: Madam Avramov, excuse me, I did not turn my microphone on. Do you have international and domestic awards for your work?

utterances.speaker: SMILJA AVRAMOV
utterances.text: Yes. I received the greatest national award, the award Dositej Obradovic, the Dositej Obradovic medal for my overall scientific and teaching contribution.

utterances.speaker: MR. PEROVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Madam Avramov, you are retired and tell us what you are doing now?

utterances.speaker: SMILJA AVRAMOV
utterances.text: I am still involved in international law. I am still publishing a lot of articles and books. I, since my retirement, I have published five or six -- six books in total and these most recent books of mine are more or less devoted to current issues. Before then, I published more legal and philosophical topics. I also published textbooks from -- on international law. Actually, that particular textbooks was published in 19 editions and is still used at all universities, law universities in Serbia and outside of Serbia too. My book, Genocide in the Light of International Law, was translated into English.

utterances.speaker: MR. PEROVIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Madam Avramov. I think that this is quite an exhaustive account of your career. In your expert report, you noted that Yugoslavia was formed in 1918 as part of the Versailles system based on military and political victories of the Kingdom of Serbia, the only sovereign state in this area at the time, and the only ally of the entente powers?

utterances.speaker: SMILJA AVRAMOV
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. PEROVIC
utterances.text: After World War II, that state was transformed into a federal community; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: SMILJA AVRAMOV
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. PEROVIC
utterances.text: On the basis of the constitution, what was the position of the federation and the federal units, the socialist republics, as the federal units of the federation? Could you please explain that to us?

utterances.speaker: SMILJA AVRAMOV
utterances.text: The position of the federal units in Yugoslavia was no different in Yugoslavia than the position of federal units in all other states that had a federative system. Meaning that at the local level, they had brought autonomy but no powers in the sphere of international law and international relations. In other words, what I want to say is that, as the only subject of international law, in international relations, you had the Socialist Federal Republic of Yugoslavia, which was the only body that had the essential attributes of sovereignty, and it alone could be represented in international organisations. It had a united diplomatic and consular representation. Only the federation had the right to conclude international treaties and, of course, to the use of military force. The federal units belonged to the federation and these were the powers of the federation that I just mentioned, and in that sense, you could say that the Socialist Federal Republic of Yugoslavia, regardless of the socioeconomic changes that ensued in the course of the revolution actually preserved a united or a specific status of a state as a single unified subject of international law. I would like to note one more thing, which is perhaps of exceptional significance, and that is that revolutionary changes which happened in Yugoslavia did not influence the international legal status of Yugoslavia because, at the Jalta conference, the three major statesmen officially, in a formal way, confirmed in writing the state and legal continuity of the Kingdom of Yugoslavia and socialist Yugoslavia.

utterances.speaker: MR. PEROVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Therefore, in the international community, Yugoslavia appeared as the only and exclusive subject of international law. Is it fair to put it that way?

utterances.speaker: SMILJA AVRAMOV
utterances.text: Yes, that is correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. PEROVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. In the SFRY constitution, and its introductory part of a declarative character, there is mentioned the right to self-determination on the part of the members of the federation. Hence my question: Does the right to self-determination include the right to secession or are these two terms synonymous?

utterances.speaker: SMILJA AVRAMOV
utterances.text: Most of the theorists, and this was particularly noted in the United Nations on several occasions that one ought to distinguish the notion of self-determination from the notion of secession of a state, that these were two different categories. Self-determination is a legal category, secession is a political category. In international law doctrine, secession was never recognised as the legitimate basis for the creation of a state. It was worked out and recognised in the Soviet doctrine and this was the consequence of Lenin's doctrine concerning the right to self-determination as including the right to secession. However, this had an exclusively ideological character because it was in this way that Lenin saw a way to destroy the so-called imperialist states. However, the European doctrines and doctrines worldwide stood firmly on the principle that secession is not a rule of international law and has no basis in international law. To this day, there is not a single rule or regulation in international law that will allow secession as the legal basis for the parting or the break-up of an existing state. Not only that. It was before the International Court of Justice that what I've just stated was confirmed. This was done in the period between the two world wars in the league of nations.

utterances.speaker: MR. PEROVIC
utterances.text: Therefore, am I right in saying that the principle of self-determination does not automatically include the right of secession?

utterances.speaker: SMILJA AVRAMOV
utterances.text: Yes, that's correct. It does not.

utterances.speaker: MR. PEROVIC
utterances.text: Madam Professor, can I just ask you to speak more slowly so that the interpreters can catch up interpreting you? Thank you. We have therefore stated that the principle of self-determination does not automatically include the right of secession?

utterances.speaker: SMILJA AVRAMOV
utterances.text: Yes, that's correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. PEROVIC
utterances.text: In your report, you stated that the acts of secession on the part of Slovenia and Croatia were counterconstitutional and violent. Why did you come to this conclusion?

utterances.speaker: SMILJA AVRAMOV
utterances.text: Above all, secession is mentioned in the 1974 constitution in its preamble, which has a declarative character. However, in the operative part of the constitution, Article 5, it is explicitly stated that changes to the borders can only take part with the consent of all the federal units and two autonomous provinces. Therefore, secession is a multilateral act. In order for it to be accepted, it has to be a multilateral act and not a unilateral act. Otherwise, as a unilateral act, it is contrary to the constitution and to the position of the United Nations. As you know, United Nations have not accepted secession as a rule of international law. It was only accepted by Moscow. Now, when the United Nations took firm position that secession can never be accepted by the United Nations, this was something stated by the UN Secretary-General on the occasion of Katanga seceding from Congo. This was confirmed later on about by several resolutions that I mention.

utterances.speaker: MR. PEROVIC
utterances.text: That is why I will not go back to them now. But as an international law expert of long standing, are you familiar with the instance of a secession that was internationally recognised?

utterances.speaker: SMILJA AVRAMOV
utterances.text: No. You see, this was a practice employed by Hitler. As you know, under the pressure of the international community, the Sudet region seceded from -- or, rather, from Poland, it was annexed to Germany. This was reversed after World War II because the international community did not recognise this. Now, in the instant case, we are talking about Yugoslavia. This was to become an area of thorough studies and criticism, of course. And I mean the secession from Yugoslavia.

utterances.speaker: MR. PEROVIC
utterances.text: Madam Avramov, how do you explain the fact that in this particular case involving Slovenia and Croatia, an exception was made? Why did the international community depart from its accepted positions?

utterances.speaker: SMILJA AVRAMOV
utterances.text: Let me just respond to why I said that this was a violent act. This because the preparations for the secession took place several years ahead of the secession itself, both domestically and internationally. A great deal was done toward that by the Croatian emigres who were very well organised and returned en masse to the country in 1990. Croatia had numerous emigres after World War II, because you know that during World War II, a Nazi Croatian state was set up with the assistance of the Nazi Germany. With the return of the emigres into the country and the setting up of the HDZ, Croatian national union, when a multi-party system was introduced, at one of the meetings of the HDZ, it was pointed out that the goal Croatia had was to go back to its original historical borders. Franjo Tudjman mentioned in the context of these original historic borders, the borders all the way to the town of Zemun or, rather, the borders that existed during the World War II Nazi-type Independent State of Croatia. Alongside the political process, there was also the setting up of the Croatian paramilitary formations in Croatia, which were widely documented, and attacks were carried out on the Serb population. Therefore, secession went hand in hand with a series of terrorist acts.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE NOSWORTHY
utterances.text: I believe that the expert had gone into an area that overreaches her expertise, but there is --

utterances.speaker: MR. PEROVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I'm not receiving interpretation into English, Your Honour or, rather, into B/C/S.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE NOSWORTHY
utterances.text: I would like to pose some questions to her at this stage. I'm sorry to intervene, Mr. Perovic, but whilst it's hot off the press and the fire, so to speak.

utterances.speaker: MR. PEROVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, I'm not receiving interpretation, and I'm not sure the witness heard what you were just saying.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, I've heard.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE NOSWORTHY
utterances.text: You're hearing me very clearly, Madam Avramov?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, I can hear you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE NOSWORTHY
utterances.text: There are a couple of questions I would like to pose to you intervening in -- at this stage. Now, you mentioned Article 5 of the constitution, is it? And the fact that it --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE NOSWORTHY
utterances.text: -- that changes to the border can only take place with the consent of all federal units. Now, correct me if I'm wrong, is there not a distinction between change in --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] That's correct.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE NOSWORTHY
utterances.text: -- border and secession. Because change in border, would it not mean whether or not, for example, Bosnia and Herzegovina tried to take -- change their borders to encroach on the territories of neighbouring states or whether Yugoslavia itself tried to overreach its territories and take in territory of a neighbouring country or state? And I see that as quite distinct from the issue of secession. Please explain for me whether you agree with that premise or you disagree and why.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No. I don't agree at all. First, I wish to say the following: The military power of Yugoslavia never went beyond the Yugoslav borders, which had been determined in several international treaties right after World War II, and the victorious forces of World War I and World War II were the guarantors of the Yugoslav borders. That is why the post Second World War Yugoslavia was the successor of the Kingdom of Yugoslavia. Secondly, Tudjman, president of Croatia and Mr. Kucan, president of Slovenia, explicitly stated and confirmed in their acts of secession that the borders would be changing.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE NOSWORTHY
utterances.text: I do not think you have got to the nitty-gritty of what I'm trying to get from you. I think the place to begin is for you to describe the process of secession or define secession and then by contrast or in addition, for you to describe what a change of border is by definition. Are you following me clearly, Madam? Learned Madam?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] From the viewpoint of international law, secession is a unilateral act whereby one country forcibly attempts to leave the community of federal units and to set up its own independent state. This is, therefore, a unilateral act which is contrary to international law, in view of the Charter which guarantees the territorial integrity of all its members. I would like to remind you, Madam, that Yugoslavia is among the founding countries of the United Nations and the signatories of the Atlantic Charter dating from November 1942. And that in San Francisco in 1945, it was stated that members who were part of the war coalition of the United Nations held a special status and that the organisation had specific moral obligations toward such countries. As far as the borders are concerned, borders are a multilateral legal act. They cannot be established unilaterally. They can only be established with the consent of the neighbouring countries and under international control. I wish to remind you, Madam, that treaties determining the borders of Yugoslavia were multilateral treaties and were never cancelled by any of the countries: France, Great Britain, United States, who were guarantors of its implementation and were never called into question by these. The determination of borders is a two-step process. The first step is to determine the borders pursuant to a legal enactment and then delineation on the part of international factors who determine precisely the line dividing the two countries. Therefore, a multilateral and a unilateral enactment.

utterances.speaker: MR. PEROVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Can I continue?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE NOSWORTHY
utterances.text: Yes, counsel, but she appeared to be saying that one could not -- initially she appeared to be saying that one could not unilaterally secede because Article 5 provides that changes to the border can only take place with the consent of all federal units and is multilateral and not unilateral.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] That's correct. Therefore, Slovenia and Croatia did an unlawful act which was contrary to the constitution and to the United Nations charter. If I may be allowed to continue, and add the following. If we --

utterances.speaker: MR. PEROVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Just a moment. Pause there, Madam Avramov.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE NOSWORTHY
utterances.text: I'm having a difficulty because she doesn't seem to be saying that there is a distinction between secession and changes to border based on that statement and that principle. I don't know if you can assist.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Your Honour, I don't know if it would be of assistance, but the constitution is in evidence. It's Exhibit 480 and if the Trial Chamber wanted to look at Article 5 in its language, I don't know if that would be of assistance.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: It is not of assistance. It is the witness's interpretation of the issues. You see, Mr. Perovic, I think what Judge Nosworthy is saying is there seems to be a contradiction contained in what the witness testifies to as the position under Article 5 of the 1974 constitution and what she says secession is by definition. Under the constitution, definition, a secession must take place with the consent of all the federal units. By definition, secession is a unilateral act. That's a contradiction. I don't know whether I've articulated what you wanted to articulate correctly.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE NOSWORTHY
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Please allow me to add --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE NOSWORTHY
utterances.text: And a further fact -- changes in the border would have nothing to do with secession specifically further.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Firstly, because the changes in borders could affect internal borders or external borders, whereas secession essentially relates to breaking away from a mother country.

utterances.speaker: MR. PEROVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I believe that the witness will be able to explain this quite clearly.

utterances.speaker: MR. PEROVIC
utterances.text: Madam Avramov, did you hear what the discussion was about?

utterances.speaker: SMILJA AVRAMOV
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. PEROVIC
utterances.text: Please, go on, please.

utterances.speaker: SMILJA AVRAMOV
utterances.text: I would just like to say that the federation was the product of the revolution, the socialist, communist revolution, and the constitution and the constitutional system were built according to the Soviet constitutional model. Secession, as I said, was of the -- a result of the socialist or communist and Stalinist system, so secession was thus included into the SFRY constitution. There is no contradiction there from the point of view of international law; secession is not permissible as a constitutional category. It was based in the ideology and if you permit, the ideological identity and international legal identity are not identical things. And Europe, in the post Cold War period, as the basic principle of its policy, adopted the status quo ante, and that is restoring the states where there was a socialist revolution to the situation before the socialist revolution. This was in force everywhere except in the case of Yugoslavia. This is where there was some confusion there, which was caused by the international community or, better said, the European Community.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Proceed, Mr. Milovancevic.

utterances.speaker: MR. PEROVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. PEROVIC
utterances.text: Madam Avramov, you pointed out the moment of the Croatian and Slovenian secession as crucial in a turning point where the crisis in Yugoslavia turned into civil war. Why do you believe that?

utterances.speaker: SMILJA AVRAMOV
utterances.text: Quite naturally, I believe that, because at the time, the so-called All People's Defence was misused. Federal units declared paramilitary units as their own regular army. And this caused a lot of upheaval and it caused, especially because there was a series of incidents and a series of confrontations, that the secessionist forces in all parts of Croatia inhabited by Serbs tried to take power violently. For example, in Plitvica, in Pakrac and in a series of other places, which led to armed conflict and these armed conflicts progressed geometrically with the injection of mercenaries, both mercenaries and volunteers. This was one aspect of it. But I have to add the international factor. The war still could have been prevented at the time. However, before war fully began to rage in Yugoslavia, in July 1991, the European Community demanded that the Yugoslav People's Army, the only legitimate military power in the country, which was a multi-national force, including generals and officers and so on, should pull back into the barracks, which made it possible for the paramilitary forces to enter even more forcefully into conflict. This was the second reason why the civil war raged.

utterances.speaker: MR. PEROVIC
utterances.text: Thank you for this explanation. But just one moment, I would like to ask you the following question. As a legal theoretician and an international law expert, what is your experience? At what point do the nationalist and ethnic conflicts acquire their most cruel and drastic form?

utterances.speaker: SMILJA AVRAMOV
utterances.text: In my modest knowledge, I always relied on important international sources and authorities and I would like to do that on this occasion, citing very prominent legal expert, Mr. Horowitz, a US theoretician and somebody who analyses current events, who wrote a lot about the situation in Yugoslavia, who said, the critical period in secession, when it turns into war, is at the point in time when one side or the other acquires international support. This is the critical point because, parallel with the proclamation of secession, Germany already in June, sought recognition for Croatia and Slovenia. The Vatican also, on its part, insisted on recognition. I would like to remind you, sir, that at the EU community, it was the community still and not union, 11 member countries of the European Community were decisively against recognition of secession. Only one country was in favour and that was Germany.

utterances.speaker: MR. PEROVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. And finally, I have one more question for you as an international law expert: Do you know whether disassociation is an international legal term?

utterances.speaker: SMILJA AVRAMOV
utterances.text: No, it's not an international term, disassociation, it's a sociological term which, in legal terminology, does not exist. It can be used as an explanation in some way but not as a concept that is accepted in law. It doesn't exist.

utterances.speaker: MR. PEROVIC
utterances.text: From the point of view of law, international law, specifically, that term means absolutely nothing?

utterances.speaker: SMILJA AVRAMOV
utterances.text: It was used, let me tell you. It was used by Tudjman and Kucan as a euphemism, as a euphemism, because I would also like to remind you about a very significant moment while the last stage of negotiations was still under way. Amongst the federal units, where all representatives, all presidents of the federal units, were invited to this meeting, this was in April or May 1991, I indicated the exact dates when this was, that Tudjman was categorically against any kind of compromise. The only thing was to constitute Croatia as an independent state, in any possible way including force.

utterances.speaker: MR. PEROVIC
utterances.text: Thank you very much, Madam Avramov. To the extent that I was permitted, I have completed my examination-in-chief. Thank you, Madam Avramov?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Perovic. It is just at that moment. Shall we maybe take a break and come back at 4.00. Court adjourned.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Mr. Whiting?

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour. First, I'd just like to inform the Trial Chamber that we have filed our response and it's been filed, it's also been e-mailed to your legal officer, a courtesy copy, as well as, of course, to the Defence.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you very much, Mr. Whiting, for that.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Secondly, I'm not sure if the report of the witness has been give and exhibit number and if that needs to be done.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: I don't think it has. Unless, of course, Mr. Perovic doesn't want it to be filed, to be admitted into evidence.

utterances.speaker: MR. PEROVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I thank you for directing my attention to this and I would like to tender the expert report into evidence, as an exhibit, and be assigned an exhibit number, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you very much, Mr. Perovic. The report is then admitted into evidence. May it please be given an exhibit number.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Your Honours, this becomes Exhibit number 1019.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you so much. Mr. Whiting?

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Good afternoon, Madam. My name is Alex Whiting. I'm one of the prosecutors in this case. Can you see me and can you understand me?

utterances.speaker: SMILJA AVRAMOV
utterances.text: Yes. I understand you.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Thank you. We have the added difficulty of the videolink here, so if at any time you can't understand me or you can hear me, please let us know, okay? Now, you are testifying here at the Tribunal as a legal expert, right?

utterances.speaker: SMILJA AVRAMOV
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: As a law Professor, as a legal expert, testifying under oath in this case, is it important for you to be careful and precise in what you write in your report that's been now admitted into evidence and what you say?

utterances.speaker: SMILJA AVRAMOV
utterances.text: I wrote the report as was my position, and I relayed my position and my firm convictions in that report, and I was governed by my work ethic which I always thought was highly important. And my work product is the product of my firm beliefs and of my studying of these areas. I have made a series of publications from that particular legal area.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: I understand that. Does -- I take it your work ethic includes being careful and precise in your legal writing, including in writing of this report. Am I right when I say that?

utterances.speaker: SMILJA AVRAMOV
utterances.text: By all means.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Okay. Now before I ask you some questions about your report, I want to ask you some questions about your views about this Tribunal, in particular, about the legality of this Tribunal. Now, in June of 1996, were you -- you were one of 24 signers of a declaration demanding that The Hague Tribunal repeal the charges brought against Radovan Karadzic; is that right?

utterances.speaker: SMILJA AVRAMOV
utterances.text: Yes. I believe it is. But if you'll allow me, I should like to --

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: We are going to look at the declaration. We have it here. It's -- it is -- if we could bring it up in the e-court and the registrar who is with you will be able to provide you a hard copy of it. It's 0115-0593. And this document is in multiple languages and you of course will look at the B/C/S version, and the English version.

utterances.speaker: SMILJA AVRAMOV
utterances.text: Sir, if you'll allow me, may I say what I have to say.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Let me ask the question first and you'll have an opportunity to answer my questions. If we, on the e-court, could turn to 0115-0600. Now, I've just lost the witness. There we go. I have her back. Madam, while we are finding the right page for us, you can look at your page at the B/C/S page, but while we are looking at -- while we are trying to find the English page --

utterances.speaker: SMILJA AVRAMOV
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: -- is this in fact the declaration that you signed in June of 1996?

utterances.speaker: SMILJA AVRAMOV
utterances.text: Yes, it is.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Do you stand by the views that are expressed in this declaration?

utterances.speaker: SMILJA AVRAMOV
utterances.text: I believe I do, fully, but I have -- I have trouble hearing.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Okay. Let me see -- can you hear me now? Are you able to hear me now?

utterances.speaker: SMILJA AVRAMOV
utterances.text: Yes. It's better now.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Okay. If you can't hear me at any point, please let me know. Do we have the correct --

utterances.speaker: SMILJA AVRAMOV
utterances.text: No, no, there are interruptions. I can hear half of the sentence and then the other half is gone.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Well, I'll try talking so that -- can you hear me now? Okay. Okay. We'll try to proceed, but do tell us if you can't hear. Does the Chamber have the correct English page of this document?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Okay, because it's not on my screen, but that's fine, because I have the hard copy. Sorry, 01150600. I don't have it on my English screen but it's -- but everybody has it?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE NOSWORTHY
utterances.text: Yes, I think so.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HOEPFEL
utterances.text: It is page 8.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Correct. Now I think it's on every screen. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: I'd like to look at paragraph 2. It says, "Attempts to exclude Radovan Karadzic from the political life of the Republic of Srpska in the period of its stabilisation." And I assume in the context that it means attempts by seeking to charge him at the Tribunal and arrest him. "Putting into effect the Dayton agreement regulations and the Paris Treaty are directly aimed at ruining Serbian people interests and represent that the attack against the democratic processes." Madam, did you -- did you believe that then and do you believe that today?

utterances.speaker: SMILJA AVRAMOV
utterances.text: Yes, sir. One ought not to forget that Mr. Karadzic took part in the entire process, from day one. Allow me to tell you that I was a member of the negotiating team since 1991 all the way to 1993.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Please stop.

utterances.speaker: SMILJA AVRAMOV
utterances.text: And that I --

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: You've answered my question. You've answered my question. My question was just whether you stand by this statement and you said yes. There is no need for further explanation. Let's look at paragraph 3 where you say, "Bringing up criminal charges against Radovan Karadzic, the president of the Republic of Srpska because of the alleged war crimes has not been grounded on facts." Now, as a law professor, and an academic and a lawyer, do you believe that that's a responsible thing to say without actually letting the process take its course, without letting a trial happen and letting the facts come forward? Is it responsible before anything has even occurred to say that the charges are not based on facts?

utterances.speaker: SMILJA AVRAMOV
utterances.text: Sir, I was a member of the negotiating team from day one, from 1991 through to the end of 1993. All the while, I was collecting voluminous documentation. I followed the developments and was kept fully abreast of the events in the territories of the Republic of Serbian Krajina and the Republika Srpska. Based on my knowledge of the time, which stemmed from my presence on the ground, I arrived at these conclusions. I would like to say another -- one other thing. I published a book on the destruction of Yugoslavia where I substantiate and corroborated the part you're currently asking me about.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: But, Madam, you cannot possibly be aware of every fact that might be relevant to the charges against Mr. Karadzic, right? So to make a statement that the charges are not based on facts, is that a responsible --

utterances.speaker: MR. PEROVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Objection, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Mr. Perovic?

utterances.speaker: MR. PEROVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I don't know what has this got to do with --

utterances.speaker: MR. PEROVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Would you pause, Madam Avramov? I have an objection to make which has to do with the relevance concerning -- with the relevance of the questions put to Madam Avramov. I don't see what her views on the alleged culpability of Mr. Karadzic could possibly have to do with the subject matter of this trial.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Mr. Whiting?

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Your Honour, the witness has been called as a legal expert in this case to express legal opinions. I think it's entirely fair for the Prosecution to explore the bases for other legal opinions and to challenge the credibility of the witness in this way. And that is exactly what I'm doing.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Mr. Perovic?

utterances.speaker: MR. PEROVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Of all the matters that my learned friend pointed out, the only true point is that he is trying to challenge the credibility of the witness in this way. Therefore, I stand by my objection based on relevance.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Well, if you accept then that he's challenging credibility, then you are overruled, Mr. Perovic, because that is perfectly within the right of the opposing party to do.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Now, Madam, would you answer my question? Was it -- is it a -- as a law professor, as an academic, as a lawyer, is it responsible to say before a trial has occurred, before the charges have been explored, before the facts have been set forth, that the charges of the Tribunal are not based on facts? Is that, in your view, a responsible position to take as -- in your position?

utterances.speaker: SMILJA AVRAMOV
utterances.text: As a scholar, sir, I had been following and studying for years the areas that you started examining when dealing with this case. Based on my knowledge of the events on the ground and the documentation that I collected, I arrived at certain conclusions. Therefore, what I stated is not in contradiction to what you are saying because you're merely at the beginning of the process of examining these events. I told you that I was on the negotiating team as one of the main members there, ever since 1991. I also took part in the conference which dealt with the setting up of this Tribunal. I don't know if I mentioned this.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Madam, when you were on the negotiating team, you were a representative -- you were representing Serbia or you were on that team on behalf of Serbia, correct?

utterances.speaker: SMILJA AVRAMOV
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Now, in paragraph 9 of this document, you say, "Bearing in mind the illegality of The Hague Tribunal." And do you stand by that position today, that The Hague Tribunal is illegal?

utterances.speaker: SMILJA AVRAMOV
utterances.text: Sir, I wrote a study which I also defended at the conference of the International Law Association in Washington. My position was then and is now that the Security Council does not have the power to set up international bodies such as this Tribunal. It can be done only on the basis of an international treaty, as was the case in the ICC, and not on the basis of a Security Council resolution. It can only establish in auxiliary bodies and that is as far as the Security Council can go.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: And Madam --

utterances.speaker: SMILJA AVRAMOV
utterances.text: And, sir, I published this study, both in English and in Serbian. This is nothing new.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: And Madam, are you aware of any decisions from this Tribunal that deal with that very issue that you are talking about? That is the legality of or illegality of how the Tribunal was created?

utterances.speaker: SMILJA AVRAMOV
utterances.text: I wouldn't be able to answer you at this time. I was following these developments. I cannot tell you now whether I am familiar with this particular matter.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: So, Madam, are you not familiar with the Appeals Chamber decision in the Tadic case dated the 2nd of October 1995, before you wrote this, which considered that very issue about the legality of the establishment of the Tribunal? Are you not familiar with that decision?

utterances.speaker: SMILJA AVRAMOV
utterances.text: Sir, on the basis of my free, legal views, I have the right to take a certain expert view which doesn't necessarily always have to correspond to yours.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Madam, you haven't answered my question. My question is: Are you familiar with the Appeals Chamber decision in the Tadic case? Have you -- are you familiar with it or not?

utterances.speaker: SMILJA AVRAMOV
utterances.text: It happened a long time ago. I cannot recall the details of the case at this time, and therefore I do not wish to speak on that matter.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HOEPFEL
utterances.text: Could we clarify when the witness -- the expert witness wrote this study and where it was published?

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Madam, were you able to hear that question? Could you tell us when you wrote that study and where it was published?

utterances.speaker: SMILJA AVRAMOV
utterances.text: I wrote the study shortly after my return from New York. That was in 1995. It was first published in Serbian in the publication of the law school in Belgrade. There, I presented an exhaustive analysis of the entire matter. It was translated into English. I can have it sent to you if you're interested. Since, as I told you, I sent it to the American International Law Association, of which I was a member.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Madam, when was it first published? You told us you wrote it in 1995. When was it first actually published?

utterances.speaker: SMILJA AVRAMOV
utterances.text: In 1995. That is when it was published for the first time.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: And do you recall when in 1995?

utterances.speaker: SMILJA AVRAMOV
utterances.text: I think it was in mid-1995. I can't tell you the date.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HOEPFEL
utterances.text: Apparently, Mr. Whiting, it was written before the Tadic decision.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] But let me tell you, I wrote very many articles after that one.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Your Honour, though, the -- I was proceeding on the basis of the fact that the witness stated that today she still stands by that view.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HOEPFEL
utterances.text: Right. Professor, may I ask you, did you write on this issue of the legitimacy of the Tribunal also later, and if yes, still only on basis of your own views or discussing the Tadic decision?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I proceeded on the basis of my own views, yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HOEPFEL
utterances.text: Thank you. Please, Mr. Whiting, you may continue.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: I guess my last question on this topic is, did you ever read the Tadic decision?

utterances.speaker: SMILJA AVRAMOV
utterances.text: A long time ago. I read it a long time ago.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: And do you recall anything about the decision or what your views were about the reasoning in that case?

utterances.speaker: SMILJA AVRAMOV
utterances.text: Sir, I wouldn't want to be discussing these matters on the basis of assumptions. I would have to have the decision before me in order to answer your question. I can't proceed on the basis of what I may or may not remember. A lawyer cannot respond to questions in that way before the Tribunal.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Could this document be admitted into evidence, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: The document is admitted into evidence. May it please be given an exhibit number.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Your Honours, this becomes Exhibit number 1020.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you so much. Mr. Whiting.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: I want to look at another document and this is one you wrote in 1996. And if we could look at 034133 -- sorry, 3430. Madam, the registrar will provide you with a copy of it in the B/C/S. We have one in English and you will have one in B/C/S, and it should be entitled "Models of Serb-hood." Do you have that in front of you?

utterances.speaker: SMILJA AVRAMOV
utterances.text: Let me tell you right away, sir, that this same document was shown to me at the time of my testimony in the case against the former president, Mr. Milosevic. This same document was shown to me at the time, and let me tell you straight away, that I was surprised at the time. I didn't write such an article. What is stated here was my speech in the association of literary writers in Belgrade on the matter of the Tribunal and proceedings and it was an extemporised speech that was translated. I don't know who wrote it down or recorded it.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Right. But Madam, in the Milosevic trial, you reviewed this document and you stated that you stand by it and that it accurately reflects your views.

utterances.speaker: SMILJA AVRAMOV
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Okay. So if we could --

utterances.speaker: SMILJA AVRAMOV
utterances.text: But not in the form of an article that was allegedly published under this title.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: I understand. We'll call it a speech. In the first paragraph, you say that the opening of the office of the so-called Hague Tribunal -- and this was in 1996 that you gave this speech, correct?

utterances.speaker: SMILJA AVRAMOV
utterances.text: Yes. I guess so.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: And it says -- you say that you "perceive the act as yet another offence to both the science of law and the honour of the Serbian people." And then in the third paragraph, you say, "the foundation of this court which is in actual fact genocidal and anti-Serbian, generated bitterness among intellectuals." Now, can you explain for us, how is the Tribunal genocidal? What do you mean by that?

utterances.speaker: SMILJA AVRAMOV
utterances.text: Sir, I am not quite certain about this genocidal part ever being within my original speech. I believe that it was inserted. But let me tell you right away, the setting up of this Tribunal embittered the lawyers in this country and above all, it embittered me as an international law expert because we believed it to have been a discrimination against the Serbian people. 220 international --

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Stop, stop, stop.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Ma'am. Doctor.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: The interpreter notes that the speakers overlap and it's impossible to translate.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] -- until the setting up of the Tribunal took place and --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Dr. Avramov. Dr. Avramov.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] -- and that was the forcible breaking up of a small country, of a small state, Yugoslavia. And I raised this issue before the international community that, for instance, the crimes that took place in Cambodia, in Vietnam, in Korea and in a number of other international conflicts, in none of these conflicts a Tribunal was set up. This only took place in the case of Yugoslavia. To me, as a lawyer, to me, as a lawyer, it strikes me as a discrimination against the people of which I happen to be a member.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Dr. Avramov, does it mean I'm being heard if I don't see her on the screen?

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: I think you're being heard.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Okay. Dr. Avramov, can I say this to you. It does not help you --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, I can hear you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Yeah. It does not help to you carry on talking when you're being asked to stop, because at that stage, you're talking, the person who is asking you to stop is talking and we don't hear what you say, so your words fall on infertile soil. So when you're asked to stop, please do stop, okay? Because otherwise you're just making sounds which are not going to be taken into consideration because they are not being recorded. We don't hear what you're saying. Now, do understand that when --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] It doesn't depend on me. It depends on --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Just listen to me. Let it also depend on what you hear, okay? When the lawyer wants any further explanation from you in addition to the answer that you have given to his answer, he will ask you to explain. If he just wants the short answer, please just give the short answer. And if he wants explanation, he'll call for it. If he doesn't want explanation and you want to give that, you can wait until when your lawyer asks you questions again and you can give that explanation at that time. Okay? Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Whiting.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Madam, just to reiterate, if you hear me say stop, and you see me put my hand up, please stop. So that we can continue.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Now, I want to focus on the word "genocidal" here. When you were shown this document in the Milosevic case, you had the document overnight, you read it and you testified in that case that you stood by what it said which you repeated here in your testimony just a few moments ago. Are you now saying that you did not say that this Court is genocidal? That that is incorrect?

utterances.speaker: SMILJA AVRAMOV
utterances.text: I think that this bit was inserted.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: But that's not something you said either in the Milosevic case or when I asked you if this was -- you stood by it a few moments ago.

utterances.speaker: SMILJA AVRAMOV
utterances.text: I stand by the text in its entirety, but this part doesn't seem to be logical. It doesn't seem to logically fit into the context into which it was inserted.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: So everything else in the text but that word genocidal is accurate, is that what you're telling us?

utterances.speaker: SMILJA AVRAMOV
utterances.text: I think that this one bit was inserted.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: And you didn't notice that when you reviewed this document during your testimony in the Milosevic case? That didn't jump out at you as a dramatic word at that time? You didn't notice that?

utterances.speaker: SMILJA AVRAMOV
utterances.text: I didn't notice that.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Otherwise, the document is accurate and you stand by it, correct?

utterances.speaker: SMILJA AVRAMOV
utterances.text: I don't understand. I didn't get your point.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Other than that one word, "Genocidal", you stand by every other word that's written in the document, correct?

utterances.speaker: SMILJA AVRAMOV
utterances.text: Correct. And I explained to you why.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: My apologies, Madam. When you say, and this is the end of the fourth paragraph --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HOEPFEL
utterances.text: Could we remain discussing the third paragraph? You picked one word out which is obviously absurd but something we heard also from a witness is also stated here. This is the Court being called anti-Serbian. And, Witness, would you -- Professor, would you stand by that also today? And if yes, do you -- are you aware that this is a criminal court dealing with individual responsibility?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] 90 per cent of those brought before this Tribunal are Serbs. The only president of a state, of all the states that fell apart, was the Serb president, who was brought before this Tribunal. Much greater blame is to be borne by a president of Croatia or Slovenia and they were not brought before this Tribunal.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HOEPFEL
utterances.text: Thank you. Sorry for the interruption. Please continue.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Actually following on from that, I'll go to the -- in the fifth paragraph, which is the last paragraph on the first page in the English, you state -- it states, just after you talk about that you were shocked as a member of the Serbian people when an indictment was issued against President Karadzic and General Mladic, the two greatest figures in recent Serbian history, you say, "I perceived the attack against them as an attack on the entire Serbian people." Is that a view you stand by?

utterances.speaker: SMILJA AVRAMOV
utterances.text: In a certain way, yes, because I know those people personally as a member of the Serb delegation. I cooperated with them frequently and I am well aware of their work. We published five or six books of documents in Serbian so far, also in English. I don't know if you have those books. The commission that published those books is called the commission for truth. And it published the complete documents relating to the activities of General Mladic and Mr. Karadzic when they were performing the functions that they performed in Republika Srpska.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Has your view that you express here about President Karadzic and General Mladic, being the two greatest figures in recent Serbian history and what you've just said, has it been affected at all by the unwillingness of these two men to come face charges here at the Tribunal in The Hague?

utterances.speaker: SMILJA AVRAMOV
utterances.text: Sir, these are completely different questions, diametrically opposed questions, that have nothing to do with each other.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: It's actually just one question. And the question is: Does your view, the view that you expressed here in 1996, about General Mladic and President Karadzic, has it changed at all because these two men have been unwilling to come here to The Hague to face the charges that are against them? It's a very simple question.

utterances.speaker: SMILJA AVRAMOV
utterances.text: It's a very simple question. I stopped all contacts with both of those people. I don't know anything about their work after the Dayton Accords.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: That's not an answer to my question. My question is: Has your view of these two men changed in light of the fact that they have been unwilling to come face the charges here that are against them in The Hague?

utterances.speaker: SMILJA AVRAMOV
utterances.text: That is their personal position that I cannot go into, and I cannot make a judgement about the character of a person based on that. That is their personal position. In the same way that there is the personal position of Bin Laden or others.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Dr. Avramov, can I just try to intervene here? Please try to listen to the question and try to answer the question as directly as you possibly can. You are not being asked to judge them. What you are being asked is whether your view as expressed in this document in 1996 has it changed or has it not changed in the light of the fact that these two gentlemen have not come to The Hague to face to the charges against them? Are you able to just -- it has nothing to do with them to say it is their personal view. Has nothing to do with their view. It is your view of them that you're being asked about. Do you have any view?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Sir, I was summoned before the Tribunal as an expert in the case against Mr. Martic. If you were to open proceedings against Mr. Karadzic, then I can be summoned to speak on that, but I would like to now just stick to the topic about which I was summoned to testify. I cannot mix up the cases of Mr. Mladic and Mr. Karadzic with the case of Mr. Martic. Let me tell you right away, if proceedings should begin against Mr. Karadzic and Mr. Mladic, then you can call me and I will give you my opinion, but this time we are speaking about Mr. Martic.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Can you -- may I stop you, please? Mr. Mladic and Mr. Karadzic are not here being tried. You are just being asked for a view on them. If you don't want to answer the question, say you don't want to answer the question. If you don't have an answer, say you don't have answer. Nobody is suggesting that you are being -- you're testifying.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: In that trial. And please listen to the questions and answer to the questions directly.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I do not wish to talk about cases that are not the topic of this particular case.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: I want to take that as saying you don't want to answer that question. Thank you very much. The record will show that.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Madam, do you understand that the --

utterances.speaker: SMILJA AVRAMOV
utterances.text: Please let it be stated in the transcript that I do not wish to talk about matters that have nothing to do with the matters about which I was summoned this time before this Tribunal. That is what I would like the transcript to reflect.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Madam, surely, as given your expertise and your knowledge about international affairs and this Tribunal, surely you are aware that the subjects about which you are asked about and required to give information -- answers to, are decided by the lawyers and the Judges at the Tribunal and not by the witness. You do understand that, don't you, Madam?

utterances.speaker: SMILJA AVRAMOV
utterances.text: Yes, but there is a limit in each case, as much as I am familiar with the practice in courts. And I was in courts before. You cannot go and exceed the boundaries of the case itself too much. You cannot go much beyond the case. I mean, I am well aware of that at least.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Madam, that is up to the Judges. It is up to the Judges here. If the Judges believe that either of the parties have exceeded -- are exceeding the boundaries with their questions, then the Judges will stop us. Okay? But until that happens, it's your obligation to answer our questions. Do you understand?

utterances.speaker: SMILJA AVRAMOV
utterances.text: But I also have the right as an expert to appear or not to appear as an expert. It is one thing to be a witness and another thing to be an expert witness. For an expert witness, you need to have explicit individual agreement.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Well, Madam -- Madam, I can tell you that under the Rules, when you start testifying, there is really no difference between the fact that you're an expert and any other witness. If you refuse to testify entirely, then there could be a decision about whether you would be summoned and what would happen with your testimony and so forth, but you're not permitted, I would say, to pick and choose which questions you want to answer and which ones you don't want to answer. Do you understand that?

utterances.speaker: MR. PEROVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] [No interpretation]

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Perovic?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I understand except I cannot understand you as a lawyer. I understand your question, what you're trying to say, but please allow me, this logic in the legal profession is something I am not familiar with.

utterances.speaker: MR. PEROVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Madam Avramov, just one moment, please. I would like to say something that I'm not sure that is an objection. I would just like to express my concern. We are coming up to the end of our second session and my learned friend from the Prosecution did not put one single question relating to the findings of this expert witness. I'm not sure that this is an objection, but perhaps it is some sort of a caution, can be taken like that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you very much, Mr. Perovic. If your learned friend doesn't go to the contents of the document, that's his choice. We'll see what he does.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Madam, I just want to give you one last opportunity, since we have talked a little bit about how the procedure works here. Do you want -- I'm going to give you one last opportunity to answer my question which is: Have your views about -- that you express about Mr. Karadzic and General Mladic in this document that you wrote -- or this speech from 1996, have they changed at all in light of the fact that these two men have refused to come to the Tribunal to face the charges against them? Will you now answer that question or do you still refuse to answer that question?

utterances.speaker: SMILJA AVRAMOV
utterances.text: I responded quite clearly that this was a matter of an individual's personal choice and not a matter for the public.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: I'm going to take that as non-responsive and not press it any further.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Could this document be admitted into evidence.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: The document is admitted into evidence. May it please be given an exhibit number.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Your Honours, this becomes Exhibit number 1021.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Now I'm not -- I do want to look at one last document on this line of questioning. I'm not going to go into it in detail, but if we could look at 03279758, and this is a document from 1997, which essentially repeats the original declaration demanding that The Hague Tribunal criminal charges brought against Mr. Karadzic be repealed. Now, I only have a copy of this in English. Do you recall that this declaration was repeated again in 1997 and that you were one of 60 signers? You're signer number 33.

utterances.speaker: SMILJA AVRAMOV
utterances.text: Yes. Yes. I recall, not just this. There were many such submissions. I can tell you that I signed at least ten. I can also say that there were about 100 altogether that were signed by legal experts or lawyers in Serbia, and that action is still continuing. It's ongoing.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Madam, you did sign this declaration, correct, in 1997?

utterances.speaker: SMILJA AVRAMOV
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: And do you stand by what's expressed in this declaration today?

utterances.speaker: SMILJA AVRAMOV
utterances.text: Probably. I should read it first, but I believe that I would stand by it. I think that it stands today.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Could this document be admitted into evidence, please?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: The document is admitted into evidence. May it please be given an exhibit number.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Your Honours, this becomes Exhibit number 1022.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Now I will turn to your report. Do you have your report in front of you, Madam? Madam, do you have your report in front of you?

utterances.speaker: SMILJA AVRAMOV
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Okay. I want to look at the first section which is called Yugoslavia and International Law and in this first section, and in your testimony here today, you state, don't you, that the federation had sole and exclusive control over the conduct of foreign affairs, correct?

utterances.speaker: SMILJA AVRAMOV
utterances.text: That is correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: And now, in reality, didn't you believe that even before 1991, there was not a single foreign policy in Yugoslavia and all of the republics were conducting their own foreign policies? And didn't you write about that in your book called, "Control over Foreign Policy"?

utterances.speaker: SMILJA AVRAMOV
utterances.text: You are right. I was deeply concerned. At the time, I was a member of the legal counsel of the Ministry of Foreign Affairs, and many times I pointed to the abuse and misuse in the case of certain republics, and I stated this before the highest organs as a danger for the future unity and integrity of the state. And in order to accentuate this in a way or stress it, I wrote this booklet on control of foreign policy, actually accusing the Ministry for Foreign Affairs of not having full control and that this was a matter that was perhaps just not deliberate or that was a question of a lack of attention on this. I also said that since Yugoslavia was a party state, a dictatorship, that the last word was in the hands of the party forums. That is why I, as a lawyer, objected to that.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: And this book or pamphlet that you wrote called, "Control over Foreign Policy," you wrote that before 1991, correct?

utterances.speaker: SMILJA AVRAMOV
utterances.text: Yes, yes. I think that it was published in 1987. I cannot remember precisely what year.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: In your testimony in the Milosevic case, you stated this, and I can show you the testimony if you like, but I'll just read to you this sentence. It's from 32403 of the Milosevic case. And my question is going to be, do you stand by this statement today? You stated, "I wrote this book entitled 'Control over Foreign Policy' in which I underlined that we do not have any control over foreign policy, that we no longer have a single foreign policy, that foreign policy is being branched off into six federal units. That was my point." Do you stand by that testimony today?

utterances.speaker: SMILJA AVRAMOV
utterances.text: Yes. That was the preparation. Yes. I stand by that and I pointed that out with the example that there was an anti-state policy being conducted that was leading to the break-up of the actual state.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Okay. And you also said, and I'm going to ask you if you stand by this, this is on the following page in your testimony, in Milosevic, 32404, you say, "I have to say that Yugoslavia was in a crisis in a certain way ever since 1945 until 1990. In a certain way, Yugoslavia was often on the brink of civil war. The cause of that was the resistance or the protest that was there." Do you stand by that testimony from the Milosevic case?

utterances.speaker: SMILJA AVRAMOV
utterances.text: Yes. I explained that later, in a more detailed article, and then I am going to deal with that subject in even more detail in a book that will be published, that I'm working on, if you're interested in all the stages of the crisis that Yugoslavia was going through.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: I think we can leave it at that. Thank you. Now, I'd like to look at the next section of your report called the "Secession of Slovenia and Croatia from the Point of View of International and Domestic Law." And in this section, and I believe also in your testimony today, you state, do you not, that the Yugoslav constitution of 1974 gives the right of secession to peoples or -- I'm sorry. Not the right of secession, the right of self-determination to peoples and not to republics?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE NOSWORTHY
utterances.text: I'm sorry. Mr. Whiting, please give an indication of the paragraph if you could or the portion or is it a general.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Yes. It's the second paragraph of that section, Your Honour, the last sentence.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE NOSWORTHY
utterances.text: Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Should I respond?

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: I just want to confirm that that's what you say in your report. If you want to look at it, it's in the second paragraph of that section that we are on now. You say that the Yugoslav constitution gives the right of self-determination to peoples and not republics.

utterances.speaker: SMILJA AVRAMOV
utterances.text: Self-determination is not a territorial principle but the subjective right of the people in essence.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: What does that mean? What does it entail?

utterances.speaker: SMILJA AVRAMOV
utterances.text: I think that, for any lawyer, it is clear what the subjective right is of a people as the bearer of sovereignty as opposed to territory which is just the object of a state.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Are you -- could you explain it in a little --

utterances.speaker: SMILJA AVRAMOV
utterances.text: One of the elements of a state.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Could you explain in a little more detail what you mean when you say, the subjective right of a people as the bearer of sovereignty? What does self-determination mean to you? If it's not territorial, what is it?

utterances.speaker: SMILJA AVRAMOV
utterances.text: It's the right of a people to express its will in relation to a particular question. For example, the system of leadership, in terms of the regime, or in terms -- ultimately, it can be, but then it must be specified also in terms of a territory, but it cannot -- self-determination cannot be linked exclusively to territory or, rather, self-determination and secession cannot be linked. I repeat, it is explicitly stated in the constitution that self-determination of people and we know what the term "people" implies and we know what federal units are as territorial units which, in essence, can have their internal borders changed also.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: So Madam, so that I understand you correctly, if you could listen to my question, do I understand you correctly to be saying that self-determination means the exercise or expression of political and civil rights in a society?
